The Ninth Air Force link (K3) is a separate later commit and is not in this pass. 38 and 46 Groups (chunk 8) are left out. Domain air. Royal Canadian Air Force heavy-bomber group of RAF Bomber Command in North Yorkshire and County Durham. rafweb group page: reformed as No 6 (Bomber) Group RCAF at Linton-on-Ouse on 25 October 1942 (formed_date; Wikipedia agrees) and moved to Allerton Park, near Knaresborough, on 1 December 1943. In June 1944 the SD161 list prints Nos 61, 62, 63 and 64 Bases (Topcliffe, Linton-on-Ouse, Leeming, Middleton St George). Nationality Canada, after the CAN-SQN rows of the RCAF squadrons; the group was an RCAF formation under RAF operational command. Id pattern of chunk 8 decision M2 (as UK-GRP-100). Bases (Nos 11-14, 31-33, 41-44, 51-55, 61-64) are not units of the dataset (chunk 8 decision M3): each squadron claim names its Base or says the station was controlled directly by Group HQ. units.unit_name: Army Group G (Heeresgruppe G; Armeegruppe G until late 1944)

units.unit_note: Improvised army-level group commanded by Generaloberst Kurt Student, formed from 1 April 1945 on the left wing of Army Group H (OB Nordwest from about 6 April) with II Parachute Corps, part of LXXXVIII Corps and the Wehrmachtbefehlshaber Niederlande (FMS B-414, Geyer, R814, German pp. 22-23 and Anlage 2, claim C9453; FMS B-674, Geyer, 'Gruppe Student formed 1.4'). LXXXVIII Corps came under it from 3 April and returned to the Twenty-Fifth Army on 6 April (FMS B-762, Prittwitz, R810, German pp. 2 and 4; Stacey, The Victory Campaign, R668, p. 550, 'Army Group Student'). On 6 April Student's staff was given the Weser defence and on 10 April Blumentritt and Student exchanged commands (B-414): the staff continues as Army Blumentritt (GER-ARMY-BLUMT; lineage UL026, 6 April 1945). Not in the Lexikon. Added 14 November 2026 (roadmap 351; Scott approved the task). Command relations: CR1314 now ends on 1945-04-06 and CR1316 (II Parachute Corps) between 1945-04-02 and 1945-04-10.

Operational command of the Channel S-boat flotillas under Marinegruppenkommando West (truppendienstlich the Flottenkommando, not entered). Formed 10 April 1942. Echelon task_group is the reserved value for a Kriegsmarine command that outranks its seekommandanten, Sicherungs-Divisionen or flotillas and is outranked by Marinegruppenkommando West (fleet). Domain naval. H2 recommended echelon other for these commands; task_group is used so the validator naval hierarchy (fleet > task_group > naval_squadron > naval_division > naval_unit) holds. Old value (as in H2): other. New value: task_group. Reason: a command of echelon other is not on the naval ladder, and a Sicherungs-Division cannot be task_group under a BdS West that is also task_group, nor can BdS West be fleet under MGK West (already fleet). The id ending 000H is not an echelon letter on a naval-ladder unit (naval_exempt), as with GER-MGW-000H. The 157th Mountain Division renamed on 27 February 1945, with nothing else changed (German Wikipedia, 8. Gebirgs-Division, R1199; English Wikipedia says the same; one source family). In Italy under the XIV Panzer Corps south of Bologna between the Reno and the Savena; early April 1945 line south of Loiano-Scascoli, Monterumici and Vado; surrendered to the Americans in April 1945 (English Wikipedia). Placeholder (leftovers-1115, task a, roadmap 363; lineage UL025): identity only, no claim. The formed date is the renaming date. Successor of GER-GEB-157D (157th Mountain Division).

The 157th Reserve Division (GER-RES-157D) reorganised as the 157th Mountain Division on 1 September 1944 (Lexikon der Wehrmacht, after Tessin; lineage UL021, claim C9455; the CMH, Riviera to the Rhine ch. 8 p. 135, has the division already transferred to OB Southwest in Italy). Reserve-Gebirgsjäger-Regiment 1 and Reserve-Grenadier-Regiment 157 were in the reserve division (Lexikon). The division became the 8th Mountain Division (GER-GEB-008D) on 27 February 1945 (German and English Wikipedia; lineage UL025). No Lexikon page for the mountain division was found (404). Added 15 November 2026 (roadmap 363; Scott approved the task). Review (leftovers-1115, task a, roadmap 363, 15 November 2026, approved by Scott, t417u): command relations added: CR1319 (Armee Ligurien from September 1944, German Wikipedia R1199, claim C9461), CR1320 (XIV Panzer Corps from 17 December 1944, German Wikipedia citing the corps war diary, claim C9462). Later history: in September 1944 the division was put under Armee Ligurien, rebuilt as a Jaeger-type division with Gebirgsjaeger Regiments 296 and 297, and held the Alpine passes from the Swiss border to the Colle della Maddalena; on 17 December 1944 it went as a reserve of Army Group C to the XIV Panzer Corps and moved to the Bologna area (staff there 18 December); in the line between the Reno and the Savena later (German Wikipedia). The Vercors operations of 1944 (English Wikipedia) are not entered. unit_note old value: said the 8th Mountain Division was not recorded and no relation; new value: this text; reason: the superiors and the 1945 renaming are now sourced.

The 1944 formation of the 16th Infantry Division (division of the 30th wave), set up in western France largely from the 158th Reserve Division (GER-RES-158D, lineage UL022) and the 16th Luftwaffe Field Division (GER-LFD-016D, UL023); formation date disputed, 4 August 1944 kept (Lexikon 16th Infantry Division and 16th Luftwaffe Field Division pages), alternates 2 July (Lexikon 158th page) and 16 August (Cole, Lorraine, p. 208 n. 6), conflict group G128 (claims C9456-C9458). On 8 August it was responsible for the Loire (Blumenson, Breakout and Pursuit, p. 560); Lexikon September 1944: LXVI Corps, Nineteenth Army, Army Group G, Epinal; commander Generalmajor Ernst Haeckel 5 August to 11 October 1944 (Lexikon; Cole has Generalleutnant Ernst Haeckel in September). Renamed the 16th Volksgrenadier Division (GER-VG-016D) on 9 October 1944 in the Vosges and almost completely re-formed (Lexikon; lineage UL024). Not the 1934-1943 16th Infantry Division (mot.), later the 16th Panzergrenadier Division and the 116th Panzer Division. Command relations: CR1317 (Army Group G from August 1944, Lexikon table row, claim C9459) and CR1318 (LXVI Corps from 7 September 1944, Cole p. 188 and the Lexikon September row, claim C9460). Echelon task_group is the reserved value for a Kriegsmarine command that outranks its seekommandanten, Sicherungs-Divisionen or flotillas and is outranked by Marinegruppenkommando West (fleet). Domain naval. H2 recommended echelon other for these commands; task_group is used so the validator naval hierarchy (fleet > task_group > naval_squadron > naval_division > naval_unit) holds. Old value (as in H2): other. New value: task_group. Reason: a command of echelon other is not on the naval ladder, and a Sicherungs-Division cannot be task_group under a BdS West that is also task_group, nor can BdS West be fleet under MGK West (already fleet). The id ending 000H is not an echelon letter on a naval-ladder unit (naval_exempt), as with GER-MGW-000H.

Lineage: its remnants formed Panzer Brigade 107 (separate record GER-PZB-107B) from 28 July 1944 (data/unit_lineage.csv UL008); the brigade returned to the rebuilt division in November 1944. Lifespan (consistency pass, branch wf-consistency-fixes, 9 November 2026, approved by Scott): the division was re-formed from 20 September 1944 at Grafenwöhr (claim C8933, Lexikon der Wehrmacht); the lineage row UL008 covers only the remnants that formed Panzer Brigade 107.

Army armoured brigade drawn from Hitler's escort battalion, commanded by Colonel Otto Remer; OKW reserve in the Ardennes offensive, committed at St. Vith, the Baraque de Fraiture, Hotton and south of Bastogne (Cole, The Ardennes; MacDonald, The Last Offensive, ch. 2); expanded to a division on 26 January 1945 (Lexikon der Wehrmacht). Echelon changed from division to brigade for 1944 (Brigades Batch 3). Formed date (consistency pass, branch wf-consistency-fixes, 9 November 2026, approved by Scott): formed_date old value 1945-01-26 (the date of the designation the record is named for), new value 1944-08, formed_date_source old value https://lexikon-wehrmacht.de/Gliederungen/Panzergrenadierdivisionen/FuhrerBeglDiv.htm, new value https://lexikon-wehrmacht.de/Gliederungen/PanzergrenBrigade/PGBFBB-R.htm; reason: Lexikon der Wehrmacht (Führer-Begleit-Brigade): the Kampfgruppe Führer-Begleit-Brigade was raised from June 1944 and enlarged to the Führer-Begleit-Brigade from August 1944 at Rastenburg and Arys; it became a division on 26 January 1945; the claim rows before the old date describe the same staff under its earlier designation, so the record starts with the staff.

Army armoured grenadier brigade drawn from Hitler's household guard; Seventh Army reserve for the Ardennes offensive, committed against the US 26th Infantry Division south of Wiltz from 22 December 1944 (Cole, The Ardennes, chs. 21 and 24; Wikipedia, Führer Grenadier Brigade); expanded to a division on 26 January 1945 (Lexikon der Wehrmacht). Echelon changed from division to brigade for 1944 (Brigades Batch 3). Formed date (consistency pass, branch wf-consistency-fixes, 9 November 2026, approved by Scott): formed_date old value 1945-01-26 (the date of the designation the record is named for), new value 1944-07-10, formed_date_source old value https://lexikon-wehrmacht.de/Gliederungen/Panzergrenadierdivisionen/FuhrerGrenDiv.htm, new value https://lexikon-wehrmacht.de/Gliederungen/PanzergrenBrigade/PGBFGB-R.htm; reason: Lexikon der Wehrmacht (Führer-Grenadier-Brigade): the Kampfgruppe Führer-Grenadier-Brigade was raised from 10 July 1944; it became a division on 26 January 1945; the claim rows before the old date describe the same staff under its earlier designation, so the record starts with the staff.

Army panzer brigade (Panzer Detachment 2105, Panzergrenadier Battalion 2105) formed on 28 July 1944 at Mielau; in Belgium from early September 1944 under the LXXXI Corps; fought before the West Wall and at Stolberg; dissolved on 23 September 1944 and used to reinforce the 9th Panzer Division (Wikipedia, List of German brigades). Brigades Batch 3. Lineage UL019: absorbed into GER-PZ-009D in October 1944 (Lexikon der Wehrmacht) (consistency fix 3, 9 November 2026).

Panzer-Brigade 106 Feldherrnhalle, formed on 28 July 1944 at Mielau; in the Trier sector from 31 August 1944; under the XIII SS Corps (September), LXXXV Corps (October), LXIV Corps (November 1944 to January 1945), then Fifteenth Army, First Parachute Army and LXXXI Corps reserves to April 1945 (Wikipedia, List of German brigades). Commander in September 1944: Colonel Franz Bäke (Wikipedia, Battle of Mairy). Brigades Batch 3.

Army panzer brigade formed on 28 July 1944 at Mielau from the remnants of the 25th Panzergrenadier Division; under the LXXXVI Corps from September to November 1944; sent against the Market Garden airborne corridor; dissolved on 7 November 1944 to rebuild the 25th Panzergrenadier Division (Wikipedia, List of German brigades). Commander: Major Freiherr von Maltzahn (MacDonald, The Siegfried Line Campaign, ch. 7). Brigades Batch 3. Lineage: formed from the remnants of the 25th Panzergrenadier Division (GER-PG-025D) (data/unit_lineage.csv UL008). End of the record: the brigade reached Baumholder on 8-9 November 1944 and was used for the re-formation of GER-PG-025D (Lexikon der Wehrmacht, R879); no lineage row, because UL008 already links GER-PG-025D to this brigade and lineage links may not form a cycle (consistency fix 3, 9 November 2026).

Army panzer brigade formed in July 1944 at Grafenwöhr; ordered to Gerolstein on 16 September 1944; under the II Parachute Corps (September) and I SS Panzer Corps (October) per Wikipedia (List of German brigades), while MacDonald (The Siegfried Line Campaign, ch. 3) puts it under the LXXX Corps of the Seventh Army on 19 September; dissolved in November 1944. Brigades Batch 3.

Army panzer brigade formed on 4 September 1944 in Wehrkreis VI; sent to Remiremont on 6 September; under the XLVII Panzer Corps, then the LVIII Panzer Corps in the Arracourt tank battles; absorbed by the 11th Panzer Division on 1 October 1944 (Wikipedia, List of German brigades; Clarke and Smith, Riviera to the Rhine, ch. 14). Commander: Colonel Heinrich Bronsart von Schellendorf, mortally wounded on 22 September (Cole, The Lorraine Campaign, ch. 5). Brigades Batch 3.

Army panzer brigade formed on 4 September 1944 in Wehrkreis V; sent to Epinal on 6 September under the XLVII Panzer Corps of the Fifth Panzer Army; destroyed at Dompaire on 12-13 September; dissolved by a decree of 23 September and taken over by the 21st Panzer Division (Wikipedia, List of German brigades; Clarke and Smith, ch. 14). Commander: Colonel Horst von Usedom (Wikipedia, Battle of Dompaire). Brigades Batch 3.

Army panzer brigade formed on 4 September 1944 in Wehrkreis XII; to Colmar on 6 September and Sarrebourg on 16 September; under the LVIII Panzer Corps at Arracourt; incorporated into the 15th Panzergrenadier Division on 1 October 1944 (Wikipedia, 113th Panzer Brigade and List of German brigades; Clarke and Smith, ch. 14). Commander: Colonel Erich Freiherr von Seckendorff, killed on 23 September (Cole, ch. 5, n. 32). Brigades Batch 3.

Special-operations panzer brigade of Otto Skorzeny for the Ardennes offensive (Operation Greif), partly in American uniforms and equipment; after the offensive stalled it was committed as an ordinary unit against Malmédy on 21 December 1944 (Cole, The Ardennes, ch. 15; Wikipedia, Panzer Brigade 150 and Operation Greif). Brigades Batch 3.

Added for German Batch 1 (27 October 2026). A provisional headquarters formed under Eberbach for the second attack toward Avranches (planned for 11 August 1944), directly under Army Group B, with a skeleton staff, while Dietrich took over the Fifth Panzer Army (Breakout and Pursuit ch. 25 p. 483); it took command in the Argentan sector on 12 August (p. 502). Wikipedia calls it the combat formation that remained in action under this title when Panzer Group West was reorganized as the Fifth Panzer Army. Not the same unit as GER-PZA-005A.

Renamed Fifth Panzer Army in August 1944 (5 August per Breakout and Pursuit ch. 22 p. 422, 1 August per Wikipedia; conflict group G020); the later name is the separate record GER-PZA-005A. German Batch 1 (27 October 2026): claims for 2 July to 5 August added. Lineage: data/unit_lineage.csv UL009 (redesignation to GER-PZA-005A).

units.unit_name: 30th Waffen Grenadier Division of the SS (Russian No. 2)
units.unit_note: Russian-manned Waffen-SS division (CMH: mutinied September 1944, reorganised; near Mulhouse in November 1944). No Lexikon page found. The 12th Army Group maps keep it east of the Rhine opposite the Kaiserstuhl until March 1945 (possibly a stale estimate).

units.unit_name: 34th SS Volunteer Grenadier Division Landstorm Nederland
units.unit_note: Low-category formation recruited from Dutch collaborationists; held the southern Grebbe Line and the flank of the 346th Division in April 1945 (Stacey, pp. 576, 581). Added 3 November 2026 for the Stacey pass; no formation date taken.

Added as a placeholder because claims name it as an opponent (engaged_with, claims C0096, C0097) and as a component of the I SS Panzer Corps (composing_units, C0160 "Heavy SS Panzer Bn 101"). Identity only: no parent, no formed date. Echelon `battalion` (review item 6; it was `other` before the vocabulary had a battalion value). The id has no echelon letter: battalions never carry one (vocabulary echelon_id_letter). Parent chain: I SS Panzer Corps (GER-SSPZ-001C), from Ellis (Victory in the West, vol. I, p. 333, mid-July 1944) and the composing units of claim C0160. No German source read names the battalion with a place; movements after mid-July 1944 are not entered (roadmap 369).

units.unit_name: 17th SS Panzergrenadier Division Götz von Berlichingen
1st SS Panzer Division Leibstandarte SS Adolf Hitler

units.unit_note: Ad hoc SS brigade formed on 29 March 1945 from training and replacement units at Sennelager and Paderborn with about sixty Tiger and Panther tanks; fought the US 3rd Armored Division before Paderborn from 30 March to 1 April 1945 (MacDonald, The Last Offensive, ch. 16; Wikipedia, SS Brigade Westfalen). Brigades Batch 3.

Sub-division unit added under Scott's rule of 4 November 2026. Traced: FMS B-023 (R843, German p.1-2, 18) lists it with the 5th Fallschirmjäger Division for the Ardennes offensive and puts Vorausabteilung 15 under its commander; an army assault-gun brigade, so attached (relation), not organic; units.csv parent_unit_id blank.

Lt. Gen. Harukichi Hyakutake. Miller, chapter IV, citing 17th Army Operations, I: Tokyo’s order of 13 August 1942 gave 17th Army responsibility for ground operations on Guadalcanal; headquarters was then at Rabaul. Hyakutake intended to command the October counter-offensive in person (Miller, ch. VI) and by mid-October had assembled a sizable portion of the army on the island.
Maj. Gen. Kiyotake Kawaguchi. Miller, chapter V: the Kawaguchi Force, nucleus the 124th Infantry under Col. Akinosuka Oka, arrived in echelons between 29 August and 11 September 1942.

Col. Kiyonao Ichiki (Miller writes Kiyono; some translations Ikki). First echelon, about 1,000 men, landed at Taivu Point about 18 August 1942 and was destroyed at the Ilu on 21 August.

Formal national command of the Dutch Binnenlandse Strijdkrachten (Netherlands Forces of the Interior; also Nederlandse Binnenlandse Strijdkrachten, NBS), entered under Scott's irregular-forces rule (HANDOFF standing rule 21) after his approval of 14 November 2026 on branch small-fixes-1113. NIMH, De oprichting van de Binnenlandse Strijdkrachten (R1163, opened 14 November 2026): on 31 August 1944 SHAEF, at Queen Wilhelmina's wish and on Prince Bernhard's urging, authorised the formation of the BS; Prince Bernhard became its commander-in-chief, under Eisenhower; on 5 September 1944 (Dolle Dinsdag) the BS was established by Royal Decree, uniting the LKP, RVV and OD. The same page records that the BS was a temporary organisation, to be dissolved three months after the German capitulation, and that it was dissolved on 8 August 1945. A second family, the Dutch Wikipedia article Binnenlandse Strijdkrachten (R1164, opened 14 November 2026), also dates the official founding to 5 September 1944 and names Prince Bernhard as commander; it gives the dissolution only as August 1945. The veterans' site binnenlandsestrijdkrachten.nl (opened 14 November 2026, not given its own reference id) cites Koninklijk Besluit Staatsblad E62 of 5 September 1944 and Bernhard's appointment as Bevelhebber der Nederlandse Strijdkrachten on 3 September, and places his headquarters first in London, later in Brussels, and in November 1944 at Breda (staff in a tax office; himself at landgoed Anneville). Those headquarters statements are not used as location claims: they describe the Bevelhebber's staff, are dated only as November for Breda, and London is not a place already in the dataset. NIMH's statement that Bernhard was under Eisenhower is not entered as a command relation to SHAEF (ALL-SHAEF-000H): a second independent family opened for this pass (Dutch Wikipedia; the veterans' site) does not name SHAEF or Eisenhower as the BS's superior, and the 16 May 1944 civil-affairs agreement on liberated territory is not by itself an assignment of this formation. parent_unit_id is left blank. The Stoottroepen and Bewakingstroepen are recorded as organic components from the 22 September 1944 split south of the great rivers (de Jong, deel 10a, pp. 561-563, R894; NIMH R1163 also names the Stoottroepen as the armed branch of the BS). Lodders and Kraandijk, Militaire Spectator 1994 (R1162): Limburg, by its relationship with the Americans, took increasing distance from Commando Zuid; the three Limburg battalions came under the Koninklijke landmacht section of Prince Bernhard's staff on 2 January 1945 and transferred into the KL in January; Brabant companies were employed by the British from 11 October 1944 and transferred into the KL in May, at which point Commando Zuid was abolished. Those transfers are noted and are not given invented end-days. No new numbered Allied parent is entered for the regional commands. Review (branch small-fixes-1113, 14 November 2026, approved by Scott): old value none, new value this unit. record_status is placeholder (old value would have been active): the unit has no claim file, because no opened source names a place for the 5 September 1944 Royal Decree, and a location claim is not invented. UK-DIST-NETH is the same pattern (a sourced higher command without a location row). The formed date and the command relations stand.

Formal territorial command of the Binnenlandse Strijdkrachten in Noord-Holland north of the IJ (gewest 11), entered under Scott's irregular-forces rule (HANDOFF standing rule 21) after his approval of 12 November 2026. De Jong, deel 10b, p. 706: around Dolle Dinsdag (5 September 1944) the lieutenant-colonel of infantry (KNIL, retired) J. G. M. Wastenecker, then gewestelijk commandant of the OD, unified the armed resistance in the district; he later appears as commandant of the BS in Noord-Holland Noord (p. 1315). Colonel Koot's orders came through well in this gewest (de Jong citing van Ojen). It published the only BS-gewest narrative in book form (De mannen van overste Wastenecker, 1947). Independent (no parent in the table; the overall BS command under Prince Bernhard and Colonel Koot is not a unit). formed_date 5 September 1944 is "omstreeks Dolle Dinsdag", when de Jong first describes Wastenecker as the district commander (then still of the OD); by April 1945 the same command is the BS gewest. The gewestelijke Stormtroepen of about 200 men (mostly former KP, p. 706) are not entered as a separate unit. Added in the de Jong 10a-1 follow-up 2 (dejong-10a1, 12 November 2026).

Formal guard and rear-area units of the Dutch Binnenlandse Strijdkrachten, entered under Scott's irregular-forces rule (HANDOFF standing rule 21) after his approval of 12 November 2026. J. van Dijk. Independent (no parent), parallel to NL-INF-STOOT. Formal combat units of the Dutch Binnenlandse Strijdkrachten, entered under Scott's irregular-forces rule (HANDOFF standing rule 21, 12 November 2026): organised with a command chain and placed at the disposal of Allied commanders. J. C. (Bep) van Kooten commander of the Stoottroepen-Limburg; van Kooten was back in Maastricht recruiting on 19 September. p. 561-563: on 22 September van Houten (not then knowing of van Kooten's Limburg appointment) appointed Borghouts commander of the Stoottroepen der Binnenlandse Strijdkrachten south of the great rivers, and gave command of the Bewakingstroepen to van Dijk; the BS were split into Stoottroepen (to fight with the Allies) and Bewakingstroepen (guard duties). formed_date 1944-09-18 is the first of the two days de Jong gives for the prince's instruction and the Limburg appointment (p. 556); the overall command south of the rivers is dated 22 September (p. 561-563). Regional command of the Stoottroepen in Noord-Brabant. First documented action: on 10 October 1944 a first company (just over 120 men) under Sjef de Groot went to the Land van Maas en Waal (de Jong, deel 10a, p. 768). De Jong later names de Groot commandant of the Brabantse Stoottroepen; he was dismissed and sent to London some time after the beginning of January 1945, after which the Brabant battalions were likewise converted to light infantry (p. 760). G. H. Bensen is named as acting commander in Noord-Brabant around 1 January (p. 760) but no appointment date is given. Organic parent NL-INF-STOOT. formed_date is the first documented company, not a separately dated charter of the regional command. Added in the de Jong 10a-1 follow-up 2 (dejong-10a1, 12 November 2026).

Regional command of the Stoottroepen der Binnenlandse Strijdkrachten in (South) Limburg, under B. J. C. units.unit_note: One continuous unit (K1 option b): RAF Fighter Command, renamed Air Defence of Great Britain (ADGB) when the 2nd Tactical Air Force was split off, and renamed Fighter Command again in October 1944 (after the window). Rename dates not stored (C18): the Wikipedia Fighter Command page says the split was "In February 1944" in its text, while its commanders table has Air Marshal Roderic Hill from 15 November 1943 and Leigh-Mallory to 15 November 1943; no source read gives a day for either rename, so no lineage row and no date. formed_date 14 July 1936 is the infobox start date of the Wikipedia page, whose text also says Fighting Area was "renamed Fighter Command on 1 May 1936". Groups in the window: Nos 10, 11, 12 and 13 (Richards and Saunders, Appendix XI). Echelon air_force. Domain air. II, p. 337, places the division, newly arrived from Italy, behind the 11th Armoured Division at Lübeck on 2 May 1945. Its service in Italy is another theatre and is not recorded.

56th (Independent) Infantry Brigade, re-formed in the United Kingdom on 15 February 1944 (Wikipedia). Independent from the Normandy landing to 20 August 1944, when it became an integral part of the 49th (West Riding) Division (Ellis, vol. I, p. 523); only the independent period has rows (Brigades Batch 1).

Moved to North-West Europe on 12 February 1945 and served under the direct command of VIII, XII and I Corps (Wikipedia, 115th Brigade (United Kingdom)); not the 155th Brigade of the 52nd Division, which fought at Flushing (Brigades Batch 1).

units.unit_name: No. 3 Naval Fighter Wing (Fleet Air Arm)
units.unit_note: Fleet Air Arm wing (Royal Navy): formed at RNAS Burscough on 25 October 1943 with 808, 886 and 897 Naval Air Squadrons; 885 joined at Lee-on-Solent in February 1944; Air Spotting Pool for naval gunfire support in June 1944 (Wikipedia, 3rd Naval Fighter Wing; Project Overlord: Cdr N Hallett, RN; attached to 2nd TAF in June 1944 mainly for administration). Reconstituted in July 1944 (886 and 897 gone) and moved to Ballyhalbert on 4 August. New id pattern UK-NFW (K9). Echelon air_group, branch Navy. Domain air. Added in the Normandy chunk 6a pass (branch normandy-raf-6a, 17 November 2026): old value none, new value this row; reason: Scott approved recommendations K1-K13 (17 November 2026).

Same headquarters throughout: constituted 14 January 1942 as II Armored Corps, redesignated XVIII Corps on 9 October 1943 and XVIII Airborne Corps on 25 August 1944 (Wikipedia, XVIII Airborne Corps). The two earlier US formations also called XVIII Corps (1921-1945 reserve) are different units.

Provisional airborne division of the Seventh Army for Operation Dragoon under Major General Robert T. Frederick: named the Seventh Army Airborne Division (Provisional) on 12 July 1944 and retitled a week later (Clarke and Smith, Riviera to the Rhine, ch. 3; Wikipedia gives 11 July). Major elements: British 2nd Independent Parachute Brigade, 517th Parachute Infantry, 1st Battalion 551st Parachute Infantry, 509th Parachute Infantry Battalion, 550th Airborne Infantry Battalion. Dissolved in November 1944 (about 25 November, Clarke and Smith, ch. 30, n. 32; 23 November, Wikipedia). Brigades Batch 2.

The 801st Bombardment Group (Provisional), the "Carpetbaggers": special-operations group of the Eighth Air Force that dropped agents and supplies to the resistance for the OSS. Wikipedia, RAF Harrington: arrived at Harrington from Alconbury on 25 March 1944 with the 36th and 406th Bombardment Squadrons, the 850th and 788th attached from May 1944; absorbed by the 492d Bombardment Group in August 1944, its squadrons redesignated (36th to 856th, 406th to 858th, 850th to 857th, 788th to 859th). Wikipedia, Operation Carpetbagger, differs on the early history (the 801st at Tempsford from the beginning of 1944, Harrington from 5 April 1944; conflict before the window, noted). Separate parachute infantry battalion. With the 1st Airborne Task Force in southern France, then in the Ardennes; disbanded 1 March 1945 (Wikipedia, outside the rows). Combined American-Canadian special force of three regiments (about 2,060 men under Colonel Edwin A. Walker in August 1944). Dragoon: Hyères islands under direct Seventh Army control, then with the 1st Airborne Task Force on the Franco-Italian border. Disbanded 5 December 1944 near Villeneuve-Loubet (Wikipedia); Clarke and Smith (ch. 30, n. 32) say it was relieved after about 25 November and formally disbanded on 6 January 1945. Recorded as US (the American and Canadian components are not split). Brigades Batch 2.

Ninth Air Force tactical air command; the 366th Fighter Group was assigned to it from 5 May 1944 (Wikipedia, 366th Fighter Group, after Maurer), and the command worked with the First Army from 17 June 1944 (6juin1944.com). Echelon corps is the nearest existing level. Placeholder: no claims of its own; it is the higher unit of the relation of the 366th Fighter Group (CR1298). Domain air. units.unit_name: Task Force A (1st Tank Destroyer Brigade)
units.unit_note: Provisional task force of the Third Army formed for the Brittany north shore railway under Brigadier General Herbert L. Earnest, headquarters the 1st Tank Destroyer Brigade, with the 6th Tank Destroyer Group, 15th Cavalry Group and 159th Engineer Battalion, about 3,500 men (Blumenson, Breakout and Pursuit, ch. 21). Under VIII Corps; soon dissolved after the fall of Brest (ch. 30). The id uses the headquarters, the 1st Tank Destroyer Brigade. Brigades Batch 2. Review: branch old value Armoured, new value Armored; reason: the US Army spelling, matching the unit name (rc1 review RV16, 24 November 2026).

Provisional mechanised task force of VI Corps under Brigadier General Frederick B. Butler, the deputy corps commander; official designation Provisional Armored Group, VI Corps (Clarke and Smith, ch. 5, n. 6). Brigade-sized: 117th Cavalry Reconnaissance Squadron, 753rd Tank Battalion (two medium companies), 2nd Battalion 143rd Infantry, a company of the 636th Tank Destroyer Battalion, 59th Armored Field Artillery Battalion. units.unit_name: United States Strategic Air Forces in Europe (USSTAF)
units.unit_note: United States Strategic Air Forces in Europe. Maurer: constituted as the Eighth Air Force on 19 January 1942 and activated on 28 January 1942 (formed_date, the US-AF-009 practice of the activation date); redesignated US Strategic Air Forces in Europe on 22 February 1944 (the present Eighth Air Force, US-AF-008 in sub-chunk 8b, is the former VIII Bomber Command); it coordinated AAF activity in the European theatre, with some operational control over the Eighth and Fifteenth Air Forces and some administrative control over the Eighth and Ninth. Echelon other, like AEAF (above the numbered air forces; chunk 8 decision M7). Id pattern of chunk 8 decision M2. Echelon other. Domain air. Added in the Normandy chunk 8a pass (branch normandy-air-8a, 19 November 2026): old value none, new value this row; reason: Scott accepted recommendations M1-M14 of the chunk 8 count, M5 widened to follow rule 26 fully (19 November 2026).
